a-theory.definition: The A-theory holds that past, present, and future are objectively different and that time really passes. The B-theory holds that all times are equally real and that 'now' is like 'here', a matter of perspective.

antinomy.definition: Kant's name for a pair of opposite conclusions that reason seems able to prove equally well when it overreaches, for example that the world had a beginning and that it did not.

apologetics.definition: The reasoned defense and commendation of the Christian faith, including answering objections and giving positive reasons for belief.

autopistic.definition: Gary Phillips's name for an apologetic strategy that treats God's word as credible in itself and the final standard, so that nothing higher can validate it.

axiopistic.definition: Gary Phillips's name for an apologetic strategy that argues from standards believers and unbelievers share.

bccf.definition: The conjunction of all contingent truths, used in van Inwagen's argument against the full Principle of Sufficient Reason.

brute fact.definition: A fact with no explanation at all: not hidden, not merely unknown, but absent.

common grace.definition: God's kindness to all people, believers and unbelievers alike, by which fallen humans still see much truly, do mathematics, and recognize injustice.

common ground.definition: The beliefs believer and unbeliever share, such as the laws of logic and the reality of the physical world, from which an argument can proceed.

contingent.definition: A contingent fact is one that could have been otherwise. A necessary fact could not have been otherwise.

creatio ex nihilo.definition: Latin for 'creation out of nothing.' The doctrine that God brought the universe into being with no pre-existing material.

cultural.definition: Defense of the faith that begins by asking why Christianity seems unthinkable to a given culture and works to make it audible as an option.

cumulative case.definition: An argument in which several lines of evidence, none decisive alone, together make a conclusion highly probable.

defeasible reasoning.definition: Reasoning to conclusions that hold by default but can be overturned by further information.

defeater.definition: A reason that, if left unanswered, would make a belief irrational to keep holding.

efficient cause.definition: That which produces an effect. Michelangelo was the efficient cause of the David.

eliminativism.definition: The view that causation is not part of fundamental reality and that causal talk is only an approximation.

entropy.definition: A measure of disorder. The second law of thermodynamics says it tends to increase, and many philosophers of physics think that increase is what gives time its direction.

ex nihilo nihil fit.definition: Latin for 'out of nothing, nothing comes.' The principle that nothing begins to exist with no cause or explanation whatsoever.

folk science.definition: Norton's term for a body of useful rules of thumb that work in everyday domains but have no place in fundamental theory.

folk theory.definition: A rule of thumb ordinary people live by, such as "heavy things fall faster." Calling a belief a folk theory suggests that experts expect to replace it, which is sometimes right and needs its own argument each time.

gethsemane epistemology.definition: Paul Moser's name for knowing God through yielding the will, as Jesus did in the garden ("not my will, but yours"), rather than as a detached observer.

hinge.definition: In Wittgenstein's On Certainty, a proposition that frames inquiry rather than being tested by it.

induction.definition: Reasoning from observed cases to a general rule: every observed beginning has had a cause, so probably all beginnings do.

inferential.definition: Defense of the faith that reasons from shared premises, such as logic, evidence, and historical method, to Christian conclusions. Technical label, axiopistic.

magisterial and ministerial reason.definition: Reason is magisterial when it sits as judge over revelation and ministerial when it serves revelation by clarifying and defending it.

material cause.definition: That out of which a thing is made. The block of Carrara marble was the material cause of the David.

mentaculus.definition: David Albert and Barry Loewer's name for statistical-mechanical laws together with a postulate that the universe began in a low-entropy state, which fix the probabilities of everything after.

metaphysical possibility.definition: What could really be the case given the natures of things. Stricter than logical possibility, broader than physical possibility.

modal collapse.definition: The result that every truth is a necessary truth, leaving no room for anything to have been otherwise.

natural signs.definition: C. Stephen Evans's term for features of experience, such as the wonder that anything exists and the sense of moral obligation, that point to God in a way open to everyone and easy to resist.

natural theology.definition: Arguments for God's existence from nature and reason alone, without appeal to Scripture. Distinct from Christian evidences, the historical case for specific claims such as the resurrection.

noetic effects of sin.definition: The effects of sin on the mind (Greek nous). Scripture describes fallen human beings as darkened in understanding, not only weak in will.

normalizable.definition: A probability measure is normalizable if the probabilities can be made to add up to one. Spread evenly over an infinite space, they cannot.

pragmatism.definition: The view, developed by William James and others, that an idea is to be tested by the difference it makes in practice. James also applied it to belief, arguing that some momentous choices cannot wait for complete evidence.

presupposition.definition: A belief one reasons from rather than to. Presuppositions decide in advance what will count as evidence.

prevenient grace.definition: God's grace at work before a person responds, making a response possible. Wesleyans hold it is given to everyone; Reformed Christians speak of effectual calling and regeneration preceding faith.

properly basic.definition: A belief held without being inferred from other beliefs that is still rational, like belief in other minds or in the past. Plantinga argues belief in God can be of this kind.

prudential.definition: Defense of the faith that asks what is at stake if one's worldview is wrong. Pascal's wager is the classic form.

psr.definition: Every contingent fact has an explanation for why it is true.

reductio.definition: Refuting a claim by showing that it leads to something absurd.

reify.definition: From the Latin res, "thing." To treat an abstraction or an absence as though it were a thing, the way a child speaks of "the dark" as a creature in the closet.

relational.definition: Defense of the faith through the visible love and changed lives of believers, summed up in Jesus' words in John 13:35.

statistical mechanics.definition: The branch of physics that explains the behavior of large systems, like a gas, from the probabilities governing their microscopic parts.

subjectivist.definition: Defense of the faith that puts the weight on encounter with God's grace and not on argument.

suppositional.definition: Defense of the faith that begins by supposing God's word as the final standard and challenges the presuppositions of the hearer. Technical label, autopistic.

tautology.definition: In the Tractatus, a proposition that is true whatever the world is like. Logic consists of them, so it shows the structure of description and says nothing about which world exists.

transcendental argument.definition: An argument that something, such as logic or morality, can make sense only if a certain condition holds. Van Til argued that condition is the God of Scripture.

verification principle.definition: The logical positivists' claim that a statement is meaningful only if it is true by logic or checkable by experience. It is itself neither, which is the standard objection to it.
